## Overview

`mcglmgraph` extends Multivariate Covariance Generalized Linear Models (MCGLM)
by structuring the residual between-response covariance $\Sigma_b$ with a
graph. Three layers are available: the Gaussian graphical model (GGM), which
parametrizes the precision matrix $K_b = \Sigma_b^{-1}$ so that its zeros are
null partial correlations; the directed acyclic graph (DAG), which uses the
modified Cholesky (LDL) decomposition under a fixed ordering of the responses;
and the completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG), the equivalence
class of DAGs that partial-correlation tests can identify, learned by
structure-discovery routines. Numerically intensive operations run in C++ via
`RcppArmadillo`.

Estimation proceeds in two stages. The first stage fits the marginal MCGLM
(mean and dispersion blocks) and extracts the standardized Pearson residuals.
The second stage forms their sample between-response covariance and fits the
graph layer to this second-order object with the Pearson estimating functions
of the MCGLM, without a joint likelihood. Graph edges therefore describe
residual conditional association among responses, not raw marginal association.
In the GGM layer, a missing edge means absence of second-order conditional
association; it coincides with conditional independence only under joint
normality of the analyzed residuals. In a Gaussian-copula model, that reading
applies to a precision matrix fitted on the latent Gaussian scale; the
Pearson-residual route does not perform that latent transformation.

```{r}
library(mcglmgraph)
```

## A worked example: recovering a chain graph

We simulate four responses whose true second-order conditional association graph
is the chain $1 - 2 - 3 - 4$, add a covariate to two of them, and fit the GGM
layer.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(1)
n <- 300
K <- diag(4) * 2
K[1, 2] <- K[2, 1] <- -0.6
K[2, 3] <- K[3, 2] <- -0.6
K[3, 4] <- K[4, 3] <- -0.6
Y <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, rep(0, 4), solve(K))
x <- rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(y1 = Y[, 1] + 0.5 * x, y2 = Y[, 2],
                  y3 = Y[, 3], y4 = Y[, 4] - 0.3 * x, x = x)

fit <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x, y4 ~ x),
                   between_graph = mc_between_graph("ggm"), data = dat)
fit
```

The partial correlations display the second-order conditional association
structure. The precision matrix used in the simulation gives a partial
correlation of 0.30 to each pair of adjacent responses and zero to the other
pairs; the estimates for adjacent pairs are close to that value and those for
non-adjacent pairs are close to zero.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
round(mc_partial_cor(fit), 3)
```

The regression coefficients are inherited from the marginal MCGLM fit. The
graph layer leaves the mean target fixed and re-expresses the residual
between-response covariance. The standard errors of the graph parameters are
conditional on the first-stage fit unless a two-stage variance is requested
(`mc_vcov_graph(type = "two_stage")`).

How much the first stage matters depends on the parameter. Suppose that the
Pearson residual of each response is $(y - \mu)/\varsigma$, with mean $\mu$
and scale $\varsigma$ depending only on the first-stage parameters and the
covariates, that the mean is correctly specified, and that the conditional
covariance of the residuals given the covariates is the same $\Sigma_b$ for
every unit. In the GGM layer, with a support that contains the nonzero
off-diagonal entries of the true precision matrix, estimating the first stage
then acts on the residual covariance, to first order, as a diagonal rescaling.
Partial correlations and zeros of the precision matrix are invariant to such a
rescaling, so the empirical (sandwich) variance of the partial correlations,
`mc_partial_cor_delta(variability = "empirical")`, and the two-stage variance,
`variability = "two_stage"`, agree to first order, and so does the null
distribution of the Wald test that an edge parameter is zero. The correction
remains for the parameters that depend on the scale: the precision
coefficients of the edges that are present and the diagonal terms. The
model-based variance agrees with the two empirical forms only if, in addition,
the working fourth moments are correct, as under normality. When the residual
correlation changes with the covariates, as it can with count responses, the
agreement is only approximate and the two-stage variance is the form to
report.

## Structure selection

In this sample, stepwise selection with BIC returns the three edges of the
chain used in the simulation.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
sel <- mc_graph_stepwise(fit, criterion = "bic")
sel$edges
```

The joint Wald test of the hypothesis that all edge parameters are zero rejects
it here. The fit is also an `mcglm` object, so the `mcglm` methods (`coef`,
`vcov`, `gof`, ...) apply to it.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
mc_test_independence(fit)
coef(fit)        # inherited mcglm method
```

## The DAG layer

The same data can be modeled with the directed acyclic graph layer, which uses
the modified Cholesky decomposition and guarantees positive definiteness. In
`mcglmgraph`, this is an ordered residual parametrization. A causal reading
requires additional subject-matter assumptions, such as a defensible ordering,
causal sufficiency and faithfulness. When no ordering is justified, the CPDAG
layer (`mc_graph_pipeline()`, `mc_ges()`) learns the equivalence class instead.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_dag <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x, y4 ~ x),
                       between_graph = mc_between_graph("dag"), data = dat)
mc_compute_criterion(fit_dag, c("aic", "bic"))
```
